items.title: 6.6 Measurement of the enthalpy change of a reaction

blocks.text: The heat evolved or absorbed during a physical or chemical change is measured with a calorimeter, which generally measures the change in temperature during the process; at its simplest it is an insulated vessel with a stirrer and a thermometer. Calorimetry relies on the fact that 4.18 J of energy raises the temperature of 1 g of water by 1 degree C.

blocks.title: Specific heat capacity
blocks.text: The heat required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance through 1 K (or 1 degree C) is its specific heat capacity, c; for water it is 4.18 J per g per K (the print also uses 4.184 and 4.2).

The energy transferred as heat is q = c x m x delta T, where q is the heat in joules, m the mass of water or solution in grams, c the specific heat of water and delta T the temperature change in degrees C, delta T = Tf - Ti.

blocks.prompt: A 150 g sample of water warms from 20.0 to 24.0 degrees C. How much heat did it absorb?
blocks.explanation: q = m x c x delta T = 150 x 4.18 x 4.0 = 2508 J, about 2.5 kJ.

items: A calorimeter (insulated vessel, stirrer, thermometer) measures heat through the temperature change; q = m c delta T with c of water 4.18 J per g per K.
